study_identification_part.si4_title: Normative modelling of brain function abnormalities in complex pathology needs the whole brain

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To introduce FUNCOIN (Functional Connectivity Integrative Normative Modelling), a whole-brain normative modeling framework for resting-state fMRI functional connectivity, and to evaluate its ability to identify abnormalities in bipolar disorder and Parkinson's disease compared to localized edge-wise approaches.

Identifying a third component in both models led to discrepancy because γ3 in the model with site effects depended to some extend on scanning site (Supplementary Tables 2-3).

nm2_modeling_method.answer: FUNCOIN (Functional Connectivity Integrative Normative Modelling): Covariate-assisted principal regression adapted for normative modeling with bias correction; log-linear heteroscedastic model for covariance matrices
nm2_modeling_method.reason: The paper provides detailed description of FUNCOIN as an adaptation of covariate-assisted principal regression with modifications for unbiased estimation. The method performs simultaneous dimensionality reduction and regression of FC covariance matrices using a log-linear model.
nm2_modeling_method.supporting_text: FUNCOIN is an adaptation of a recently developed method from statistics literature, covariate-assisted principal regression, which performs simultaneous dimensionality reduction and regression of covariance matrices... FUNCOIN, which we released in a Python package, finds FC components (i.e. linear projections) that are maximally related to sex and age (or other specified covariates) while respecting the mathematical (positive semidefinite) structure of the FC matrix... The model is a log-linear, heteroscedastic model for covariance matrices...

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Answer: FUNCOIN whole-brain normative modeling successfully identified abnormal functional connectivity patterns in PD (9.1% outliers, p=0.002) and BD (6.9% outliers, p=0.046), including detection of PD abnormalities up to 8 years before diagnosis, while localized edge-wise approaches failed to identify individual-level deviations after multiple comparison correction.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Answer: In the whole-brain FUNCOIN model, 9.1% of PD subjects had Z1<-2 (significantly more than expected 2.3%, padj=0.002), indicating decreased magnitude of component 1 which includes structures previously shown affected in PD (nucleus caudatus, thalamic and cerebellar networks). For BD, 6.9% had Z2<-2 (padj=0.046) and 7.9% had Z1>2 (padj=0.09, did not survive FDR correction). Notably, none of the BD subjects had both Z1>2 and Z2<-2, suggesting two distinct subgroups with effective prediction accuracy of 14.8%. Component 2 includes medial and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex with opposite signs, compatible with known lack of anticorrelation in BD. Remarkably, among 54 PD subjects scanned up to 7.8 years before diagnosis, 9.3% were outliers (padj=0.01), with outliers scanned on average 3.2 years before diagnosis. In contrast, localized edge-wise models (analyzing 1485 unique connections) could not identify individual outlier subjects after multiple comparison correction using Benjamini-Yekutieli procedure, despite group-level differences detected by summarizing Z-scores (e.g., Mann-Whitney U showing distribution differences in outlier counts). Edge-wise Z-scores showed minimal between-subject correlation (mean Spearman r=0.01-0.02 for BD/PD vs. 0.0005 for healthy), indicating lack of specific shared deviation patterns. The two best-fitting edge-wise models (R²=0.10 and 0.09) showed no significant difference in outlier proportions between diagnostic and healthy groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Answer: FUNCOIN addresses major limitations of edge-wise normative modeling: (1) avoids massive multiple testing problem (2,970 hypotheses per subject reduced to 4 tests for 2 components in 2 directions), (2) provides interpretable whole-brain components mapping onto known networks (e.g., default mode, striatal/thalamic/cerebellar), (3) increases statistical power and specificity by focusing on covariate-related dimensions, (4) scales well (trained on 32,000 subjects with 55 ICA components in <25 minutes with linear time scaling). Components are orthogonal and sign-invariant, providing distinct dimensions for subtyping heterogeneous patient populations. Potential for clinical screening of at-risk individuals (e.g., genetic susceptibility to PD) and for longitudinal tracking of Z-score changes. Released as open-source Python package with comprehensive documentation.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Answer: Preprint status (not peer reviewed); single dataset (UK Biobank) without external validation limiting generalizability; limited reporting on image-level quality control and motion parameters; model captures linear log-linear effects on FC component magnitudes but may miss nonlinear age/sex effects or higher-order interactions; interpretation of Z-score clinical relevance requires consideration of artifact, chance, and intervention effects; some disease subjects may be undetectable if starting from extreme end of normal spectrum; no repeated scans analyzed (though longitudinal methods adaptable); age and sex distributions for clinical groups not reported

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a preprint (bioRxiv, posted August 21, 2025) introducing FUNCOIN as a novel whole-brain normative modeling framework for functional connectivity. The method adapts covariate-assisted principal regression with bias correction modifications. Data from UK Biobank with 4 scanning sites, harmonized acquisition on Siemens Skyra 3T. Full dataset includes 55 ICA component time series with 490 time points. Model trained on 32,000 healthy subjects, validated on 14,000 healthy subjects, and tested on BD (n=101) and PD (n=132) groups. Two FUNCOIN components identified: Component 1 (R²=0.32, associated with sex and age) includes default mode network, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, thalamus, retrosplenial cortex, cerebellum, and striatal structures. Component 2 (R²=0.24, mainly sex-associated) includes default mode network, temporoparietal junction, parahippocampal gyrus, medial and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Model validation showed consistency (N≥2,000 sufficient for first two components), unbiasedness (after correction), statistical validity (normal residuals, homogeneous variance), good calibration (out-of-sample Z-scores: skew=0.21/0.02, excess kurtosis=-0.14/-0.21), and excellent scalability. Site sensitivity analyses showed first two components robust to site inclusion. Comparing to edge-wise approaches: best edge models had R²=0.10 and 0.09 vs. FUNCOIN R²=0.32 and 0.24; 3.8% and 9.8% of unadjusted p<0.05 for BD and PD respectively in edge-wise tests, but all adjusted p>0.15 after Benjamini-Yekutieli correction. Heterogeneity in edge-wise outlier patterns suggests noise rather than true disease heterogeneity. Limitations in detecting individual outliers with summarization methods (outlier counting, extreme value distributions) despite group-level differences. Python package (FUNCOIN) available at https://github.com/kobbersmed/funcoin with pip installation option. Analysis code and README available at https://github.com/kobbersmed/Paper_Normative_modelling_of_brain_function. Visualization performed with FSL fsleyes v1.12.6, statistics with scipy v1.13.1 and scikit-learn v1.5.1. Full list of datasets where subjects were considered healthy: no ICD-10 category F or G diagnoses (~50,000 of >60,000 subjects). Time of diagnosis for clinical groups determined from first occurrence in health records.
